title: Week 5 — PD1: What the courses don't tell you
tweets:
I've seen smart people fail PD1 three times in a row.

not because they couldn't code.

because they studied Apex like a Java course instead of a Salesforce exam.

here's what actually matters 🧵

the exam doesn't care if you can build an app.

it cares if you know what breaks when your code runs on a million records at once.

every scenario question is secretly asking: 'what governor limit is being violated here?'

if you don't see that, you're reading it wrong.

three patterns that answer maybe 40% of the exam:

- SOQL inside a for-loop → wrong
- DML inside a for-loop → wrong
- hardcoded IDs in code → wrong

they'll phrase these 8 different ways. you need to recognize the pattern, not memorize the phrasing.

test classes trip up so many people.

the thing that costs people points: not knowing that Test.startTest() / Test.stopTest() resets your governor limits inside the block.

also: System.assertEquals(expected, actual) — expected goes FIRST. I know it feels backwards. it is backwards. memorize it anyway.

real talk: PD1 is a comprehension exam, not a coding exam.

you don't write code. you read code and answer 'what happens when this runs?'

big difference. if you've been writing Apex to study, you might be over-engineering your prep.

title: Week 5 — Which cert should you get first (honest answer)
tweets:
everyone asks me which Salesforce cert to get first.

and everyone expects me to say 'it depends.'

but I'm going to give you a real answer instead.

🧵

if you are completely new to Salesforce:

Admin. full stop.

not because it's easiest. because every other cert assumes you already know what a profile is, how OWD works, and what a validation rule does.

skipping Admin is like skipping grammar to study literature. you can try. it just takes twice as long.

if you're already an Admin and wondering what's next:

stop and ask yourself ONE question first.

'what role do I actually want to be hired into in 12 months?'

the answer to that question IS your next cert. not what's trending. not what your manager has. what you want to do.

the mistake I see constantly:

people collecting certs they'll never use because someone on LinkedIn said they were valuable.

I've spoken to people with 8 certs who can't get an interview.
and people with 2 certs who had 3 offers.

the difference was relevance, not quantity.

if I had to pick 3 certs that give the most leverage in 2026:

1. Admin — opens every door, prerequisite for nearly everything
2. Agentforce Specialist — almost nobody has it yet, demand is rising fast
3. Sales Cloud Consultant — every SF implementation has this role

not the most glamorous list. but the most hireable one.

one more thing nobody tells you:

Salesforce certs expire. you need to pass maintenance exams every year to keep them active.

so 8 certs means 8 maintenance exams every year. that's a real time commitment.

get fewer certs you actually use. go deep on those.

title: Week 5 — I failed ADM-201 three times
tweets:
I failed ADM-201 three times.

attempt 1: 57%
attempt 2: 63%
attempt 3: 61%

I studied every single day. I wasn't slacking. I was doing everything everyone told me to do.

and I kept failing.

here's what I eventually figured out 🧵

first attempt: I did every Trailhead module in order. all 80+ of them.
6 weeks. probably 200+ hours.

got to the exam and it felt completely different from anything I'd studied.

I thought the exam was broken. it wasn't.

second attempt: bought a Udemy course. watched every video. took detailed notes.

was more prepared. still failed.

third attempt: bought two practice test banks. did every single question. memorized the explanations.

scored lower than attempt 2.

that one really stung.

I almost quit after attempt 3.

then someone said something that stuck:

'you're memorizing correct answers, not understanding why they're correct.'

I'd been using practice tests to test myself instead of using them to FIND what I didn't understand.

completely different activity.

attempt 4 looked like this:

day 1: did a full practice exam cold. didn't study anything first.
marked every question I wasn't 100% sure on, even the ones I guessed right.

then: for every single flagged question — found the official Salesforce documentation and read it.

not a summary. the actual docs.

then did the practice exam again. only paid attention to my weak sections.

kept repeating until I was consistently getting those sections right.

didn't touch the topics I already knew.

attempt 4: 84%.

not because I studied more. because I stopped studying what I already knew.

the method: diagnose → learn the concept → verify.

not: study everything → hope → test.

the exam is not testing your memory. it's testing whether you understand WHY one approach is better than another in a specific situation.

that's a different skill than memorization.

if you've failed an SF exam: you're probably not studying wrong topics. you're studying in the wrong way.

title: Week 6 — Agentforce Specialist: how to actually study for it
tweets:
Agentforce Specialist might be the smartest cert to get right now.

not because it's easy. because almost nobody has it yet.

I mapped out exactly how I'd study for it if I were starting today.

🧵

first: ignore the hype and understand what the exam is actually testing.

it's not about whether you can code AI.

it's about whether you can configure an Agent correctly — set up Topics, write Instructions, build Actions, test behavior — and know WHEN to use an Agent vs a Flow vs just a bot.

the exam breakdown:

Agent Building: 35% (the biggest section by far)
Agent Design: 22%
Agentforce Concepts: 17%
Testing & Debugging: 14%
Evaluate and Iterate: 12%

notice that 35% is hands-on building. you cannot pass this section by reading about it.
you have to actually build agents in a developer org.

the section that trips people up: Agent Design.

it's full of scenario questions like 'a customer is asking X, what should the agent do?'

those questions aren't testing your technical knowledge. they're testing whether you understand what an agent is supposed to be GOOD at vs what it should hand off to a human.

the Testing & Debugging section has a specific pattern I noticed:

every debugging question follows the same logic:
topic routing first → action inputs second → the action itself third.

if the agent gives a wrong answer, you always start at the top of that chain and work down.

know that and you'll get those questions right.

the single most underused resource for this exam:

Salesforce's actual implementation guides for Agentforce.
not the marketing pages. the 'how to configure' documentation.

spend 2-3 hours in there and you'll understand the exam structure better than most study guides explain it.

title: Week 6 — Spring '26 is here. Here's what changed for your exam.
tweets:
Spring '26 just dropped.

if you're studying for a Salesforce cert right now, some of your material might already be outdated.

here's what actually changed and how to know if it affects YOUR exam 🧵

#Spring26 #SalesforceCertification

quick background on why this matters:

Salesforce updates exam outlines 1-3 times a year to reflect new features.

if your study guide hasn't been updated, you could be preparing for questions that no longer exist — or completely missing new ones that just got added.

what changed in Spring '26 that actually shows up on exams:

Agentforce: multi-agent orchestration is in. if you're studying Admin or Agentforce Specialist, expect scenario questions about how agents hand off to each other.

Flow: new debugging and orchestration tools. the 'how do you debug a failing flow?' question just got more nuanced.

Data Cloud: real-time data activation and identity resolution got expanded.

if you're studying Data Cloud Consultant, governance and unification are heavier now.

Tableau: Pulse features for proactive analytics. Tableau exams may reference these in data storytelling questions.

what hasn't changed and probably never will:

the security model. governor limits. declarative-first philosophy. sharing and visibility architecture.

these make up 40-60% of most exams and they barely move between releases.

if you're cramming, start here. always.

how to check if YOUR exam changed:

1. search '[cert name] exam guide' on Trailhead
2. find the 'Last Updated' date
3. compare section weights to your study guide

if they don't match: trust the official guide.

no course vendor updates faster than Salesforce does.

title: Week 7 — Should Admins move to Developer?
tweets:
Admins always ask me: should I become a developer?

my honest answer: probably yes. but not for the reasons you think.

🧵

the obvious reason to do it: developer salaries start $15k-$25k higher than admin salaries at entry level.

but that's not actually why I'd recommend it.

I'd recommend it because the Salesforce dev path has a clear ceiling — Architect — and Architects earn real money.

the part nobody tells you:

if you already know Flow well, you're maybe 40% of the way to understanding Apex.

the logic is the same. variables, decisions, loops, calling other things.

Apex is just Flow with curly braces and stricter rules.

most Admins are closer to this than they realize.

what 'Admin to Developer' actually looks like in practice:

you'll spend 2-3 months feeling slow and stupid while Apex syntax clicks.

then it clicks. and you realize your Admin knowledge just became a superpower — because you understand the platform developers are building on.

the case for NOT switching (and nobody says this enough):

if you're excellent at Admin + configuration + process consulting, the Solution Architect path might pay MORE than the pure Developer path.

business-side Architects can earn as much as technical ones. different route to the same ceiling.

if I were an Admin today deciding whether to go Developer:

1. get App Builder first. it's 4-6 weeks from your existing knowledge and proves you can go deeper.
2. take a week to try writing a basic Apex trigger. see if you enjoy it.
3. if yes: PD1. if no: Consultant or Architect track.

don't decide in the abstract. try it first.

title: Week 8 — What Salesforce exam day is actually like (14 exams in)
tweets:
I've taken 14 Salesforce certification exams.

the first one I nearly failed the check-in process before the test even started.

here's everything I wish I'd known about exam day before attempt 1.

🧵

#SalesforceCertification

you take the exam from your own computer via Kryterion Webassessor.

a live human proctor watches you through your webcam the whole time.

they will ask you to show them the room. they will ask you to remove things from your desk. they take this seriously.

clear your space the night before.

the check-in process takes 15-20 minutes.

if you log in at your exact exam time, you're already behind.

log in 30 minutes early. every time. without exception.

also: test your webcam and mic the night before. a technical issue 10 minutes before your exam is a very bad way to start.

the thing that trips up first-timers most: the question wording.

Salesforce doesn't ask 'what is the right answer?'

it asks 'what is the BEST approach?' or 'which is MOST appropriate?' or 'what is LEAST likely to cause issues?'

this matters. two answers can both be technically correct. only one is the most Salesforce-aligned.

how to handle questions you're stuck on:

1. cross out the two obviously wrong answers first
2. from the remaining options: which is more declarative / native to Salesforce?
3. which protects data integrity better?
4. still stuck? mark it and move on. come back later with fresh eyes.

never spend more than 90 seconds on a question the first time through.

the night before: do one practice exam, clear your desk, check your login.

that's it.

no new material. no cramming. if you don't know it by the night before, two more hours won't save you.

sleep is more useful than one more Trailhead module at 11pm.

what to do if you fail:

get your score report — it shows exactly which sections you failed.
wait a day before you decide anything.
then study ONLY the weak sections. don't restart everything.

you can retake after 1 day (first retake) or 14 days (subsequent). most people pass the retake once they know where they actually failed.
